title: Sri Lanka Retail Forum 2026 - Retail without boundaries: Building next growth engine | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 05:34
-     - 42

Sri Lanka Retailers’ Association President Infiyaz Ali

The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Chairperson Krishan Balendra

Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India Partner Soumya Dwibedi

Centre for Poverty Analysis Consultant Dr. Roshan Perera

USJ Postgraduate Institute of Management Director Dr. Asanga Ranasinghe

Havelock City Mall Marketing and Leasing General Manager Avanthie De Zoysa

Ceylon Biscuits Director and Chief Executive Officer Nalin Karunaratne

The Hotels Association of Sri Lanka Chief Executive Officer Priantha Fernando

PepperCube Consultants Chief Insights Officer and Executive Director Crystal Nathan (Moderator)

Modern trade forecast to reach no more than 40% of retail over the next decade

 India’s growth seen as a major opportunity for Sri Lanka’s retail sector

Consumer data, regional markets and technology emerge as key drivers of retail growth 

 Sri Lanka targets 5 m tourists by 2030 as industry seeks higher-value visitors

 Tourism spending needs to rise at least to $ 200 per visitor, per day

 Tourism calls for stronger infrastructure and more targeted marketing in key markets

By Safna Malik

The Sri Lanka Retailers’ Association (SLRA), in partnership with the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, last week successfully concluded the Sri Lanka Retail Forum 2026 under the theme “Retail Without Boundaries: Building the Next Growth Engine”, bringing together retailers, business leaders and industry experts to explore the changes shaping Sri Lanka’s retail sector and its next phase of growth.

Speaking at the event, Sri Lanka Retailers’ Association (SLRA) President Infiyaz Ali said the theme ‘Retail Without Boundaries: Building the Next Growth Engine’ reflected where the retail sector needed to go as geopolitics, technology and climate change continued to reshape the business environment.

Retailers need to adapt fast enough to keep growing instead of just keeping up - SLRA President Infiyaz Ali

The forum provided an opportunity to learn from other markets and consider what could be applied in Sri Lanka, as retailers faced a rapidly changing business environment. “Retailers need to adapt fast enough to keep growing instead of just keeping up,” he said.

He also pointed to SLRA’s membership in the Federation of Asia Pacific Retailers Association, which gave its members access to a network spanning 18 countries across the Asia Pacific region.

Addressing the forum as the Chief Guest, Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Chairperson and John Keells Holdings PLC Chairperson Krishan Balendra said Sri Lanka had made important progress in economic stabilisation, with inflation moderating, foreign exchange availability improving and interest rates falling. However, he stressed that recovery alone was not enough and the next priority was sustainable growth.

Recovery alone is not enough. The next priority is sustainable growth - Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Chairperson and John Keells Holdings Chairperson Krishan Balendra

Balendra said policy consistency and predictability were essential for investment and called for Sri Lanka to maintain its reform momentum beyond the current IMF-supported program. Continued reforms, he said, would strengthen policy credibility, support growth and resilience, and improve access to international investment.

Turning to trade, he said Sri Lanka needed greater integration with regional and global markets through stronger exports, improved logistics, modernised customs, simpler regulations and investment facilitation. The removal of para tariffs was a welcome first step, but broader reforms were needed to make the country more competitive.

He also stressed the need to help medium-sized enterprises scale up through better access to finance, technology, skills and export opportunities, saying they could become the next generation of national businesses.

Pointing to Sri Lanka’s location in the Indian Ocean, Balendra said its proximity to India could become a major source of future economic growth. Indian tourist arrivals had increased from around 150,000 a decade ago to more than 500,000 last year, while around 85% of Colombo Port’s volume was transshipment, much of it linked to India.

India’s growth could have a similar impact on Sri Lanka to the benefits neighbouring countries gained from China’s rapid growth two decades ago. The retail sector, he added, would play an important role in this broader economic growth by supporting employment, innovation and consumer demand.

The keynote sessions covered key areas shaping the future of retail, beginning with Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India LLP Partner Soumya Dwibedi, who addressed retail as a growth engine, regional and global shifts in go-to-market strategies, business transformation and the structural changes needed to support Sri Lanka’s retail expansion.

The Centre for Poverty Analysis Consultant Dr. Roshan Perera focused on productivity and performance, covering operational bottlenecks, efficiency and fiscal policies affecting retail sector growth. 

The Postgraduate Institute of Management, University of Sri Jayewardenepura Director Dr. Asanga Ranasinghe addressed customer experience, brand leadership and building trust and loyalty through human connections.

The 1 Central Group Senior Vice President Hansa Wongsiripitack spoke on the future of retail and loyalty through a case study of The 1, Thailand’s digital lifestyle and loyalty platform connecting customers with Central Group businesses and partner brands. She demonstrated how loyalty programs could go beyond points and rewards by connecting customer data, personalised experiences and multiple touchpoints. The session also highlighted how a 360-degree customer view could strengthen engagement.

The most important thing is being relevant: how relevant are you to your consumer and to your target audience? - Havelock City Mall General Manager Marketing and Leasing Avanthie De Zoysa

A key highlight of the forum was the ‘Tech and Future Retail’ panel, featuring Havelock City Mall General Manager - Marketing and Leasing Avanthie De Zoysa, Ceylon Biscuits Ltd. Director and CEO Nalin Karunaratne, and The Hotels Association of Sri Lanka (THASL) CEO Priantha Fernando. The session was moderated by PepperCube Consultants Chief Insights Officer and Executive Director Crystal Nathan.

Phygital customer journey 

De Zoysa said the mall combined its physical and digital customer experience. “In the shopping mall, we map the digital experience with the customer journey when a customer walks into the mall,” she said.

She said the journey began with vehicle recognition at the entrance. Instead of taking a parking ticket, the system recognised the vehicle number plate, showed available parking spaces to guide customers. Directional boards and mall directories were also introduced to help customers find their way around the mall and locate stores.

Once customers made a purchase, they could provide their mobile number to earn loyalty points. This allows the mall to track customer shopping patterns, including the stores they visited, how often they visited, how much they spent and what they bought.

This collected information is then used to send location-based notifications, such as promotions on customers’ favourite brands. The mall could also track how long customers stayed and reach out to with offers from their preferred brands. “So, from the time you enter the mall until you leave, the journey is connected,” she said. There is personalisation throughout the journey. Adding,  Malls power the economy through taxes, job creation and revenue generation.

AI, big data and Sri Lanka tourism

Speaking about the future of Sri Lanka’s tourism industry, Fernando said the country still had a long way to go in adopting technology compared with more developed markets.

He said hotels needed to use technology better to maximise revenue, particularly because an unsold room meant lost income that could not be recovered. In other countries, hotel prices changed according to demand and room availability, allowing operators to adjust rates. “The industry embraces the latest era of technology,” he said, stressing the need for tourism businesses to move towards digital transformation.

Digital change was also reshaping the travel sector, he said, as travellers increasingly chose their destinations and travel arrangements themselves. DMCs and travel agents therefore needed to make information available online before visitors travelled.

Fernando said the share of business coming into Sri Lanka through DMCs and online travel agencies (OTAs) had fallen from around 81% four or five years ago to around 36% today. This meant DMCs would need to adapt their services to changing consumer behaviour.

Travel apps were also changing how tourists chose places to visit, shop, eat and find entertainment. Service providers across the tourism sector would therefore need to adapt as technology developed.

With Sri Lanka targeting five million tourists by 2030, compared with around 2.3 million currently, Fernando said the country also needed to increase tourist spending. Average daily spending was around $ 156 and needed to reach at least $ 200, he said, with more opportunities created through services and entertainment.

Sri Lanka had been catering more towards budget tourists, he said, while only 10,000 to 12,000 of the country’s approximately 55,000 formal hotel rooms were suitable for the high-end market. These hotels were already recording occupancy levels above 75% to 80%.

My prediction for the next 10 years is that modern trade will not be more than 40% - Ceylon Biscuits  Director/CEO Nalin Karunaratne

Fernando also said Sri Lanka had not sufficiently targeted markets such as Japan, Australia and South Korea. Greater focus on these markets could help balance seasonal trends in tourism.

Modern trade growth

Turning to the future of modern trade, Ceylon Biscuits Ltd. Director and Chief Executive Officer Nalin Karunaratne said modern trade now accounted for around 18% to 25%, depending on the category and segment.

“Twenty-five or 26 years ago, the ratio was almost 90% general trade, with only around 10% to 12% modern trade or self-service,” he said. It had therefore taken about 25 years for modern trade to almost double its share.

Karunaratne predicted that modern trade would account for no more than 40% over the next 10 years. “My prediction for the next 10 years is that modern trade will not be more than 40%,” he said.

Legal and policy restrictions on international retail chains entering Sri Lanka could limit further growth, he said. However, local modern trade operators were “second to none” in their offerings and propositions, with more players entering the sector.

Convenience was another factor shaping consumer behaviour. Sri Lanka has around 220,000 retail outlets, with many located close to homes. A one-kilometre drive in Sri Lanka could also take almost twice as long as the same distance in Malaysia, he noted.

Small and medium-sized retailers and neighbourhood outlets were therefore growing faster than modern trade in some areas. The high cost of expanding modern trade was another factor, with larger outlets concentrated mainly in the Western Province and its outskirts, where customer traffic could support faster returns.

Karunaratne also pointed to per-capita income as a factor in the shift towards modern trade. Sri Lanka had not yet seen the level of economic transformation expected at higher income levels, he said, which was why he continued to stand by his 40% prediction.

Consumer data shaping mall retail

Speaking about how consumer behaviour data was influencing tenant selection and retail space design, De Zoysa said consumer data guided its choice of brands and stores.  “Modern-day shoppers give us feedback through the many touchpoints available to them,” she said, adding that these touchpoints helped the mall understand consumer preferences.

“The most important thing is being relevant: how relevant are you to your consumer and to your target audience?” De Zoysa said, adding that staying relevant required the mall to keep evolving. Data guided the choice of brands, changes to its store mix and store sizes, as well as the balance between food and beverage (F&B) and non-F&B outlets. “Most of our changes are therefore driven by consumer data,” she said.

Tourism infrastructure and marketing

Explaining the infrastructure gap, Fernando said improvements would be needed to support the country’s plans for high-end tourism, highlighting the need for better accommodation and infrastructure.

Fernando said there was strong demand for Sri Lanka, noting that South Asia was seeing some of the highest tourism demand globally, with around 7% to 8% of global tourist movements, while the country had yet to gain its full potential in the regional market.

South Asia is seeing some of the highest tourism demand globally, but Sri Lanka has yet to gain its full potential in the regional market - THASL CEO Priantha Fernando

Pointing to marketing as a key gap, he said Sri Lanka had not carried out proper marketing in its key generating markets. Much of the growth had been natural, with hoteliers and destination management companies (DMCs) promoting the destination, while tourism authorities needed to take a more planned approach.

Turning to visitor spending, Fernando said Sri Lanka could increase its prices. “We have to create more opportunities for them to spend their money,” he said. Sri Lanka remained reasonably priced while the quality of its offering had improved, he said. The change in the dollar exchange rate had also increased tourists’ buying power.

FMCG growth beyond volume

Karunaratne said consumers today have access to a great experience, while the same products are often replicated. Some companies were creating products for specific segments and positioning them differently from their mainstream portfolio.

He also pointed to companies developing their own house brands, which could pose a threat to existing players. One way to respond, he said, was to focus on a hero product rather than have an entire product portfolio in every segment. “One hero product can suffice,” he said.

The discussion continued through a series of special sessions, with Singer (Sri Lanka) PLC Group Managing Director Mahesh Wijewardene sharing the company’s transformation playbook, including category expansion, retail execution, brand modernisation and strategies to stay relevant in a changing economy. 

Meanwhile, Finetech Consultancy Ltd. Group Director, Group CEO and Co-Founder Clehan Pulle explored AI-enabled customer service, including automated call handling, digital support queues and cloud solutions to improve productivity and reduce operating costs. 

Barista Coffee Lanka  Ltd. Chief Executive Officer Dilupa Pathirana then shared lessons from Barista’s growth journey, focusing on how continuous learning could support retail expansion. The overall forum offered retailers the opportunity to create more connected experiences and explore new avenues for growth.

title: Colombo has the opportunity; now Sri Lanka must execute: Global maritime leaders | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 04:24
-     - 142

American cargo doesn’t begin its journey when it reaches one of our ports. It often begins thousands of miles away, frequently in a place like Sri Lanka

— US FMC Commissioner Robert J. Harvey

The real transformation happens when you combine a hub with strong logistics capability. That combination creates an ecosystem far bigger than the sum of its parts, and it’s also what attracts FDI

—AP Moller (Maersk) Singapore Managing Director René Piil Pedersen

Fashion moves so fast now that a garment has almost become perishable: if it doesn’t arrive on time, it loses its value

—Brandix Lanka CEO 

Ashroff Omar

This isn’t purely altruistic support for Sri Lanka’s ports; it’s a genuine win-win for both economies

—US Embassy in Colombo Indo-Pacific Coordinator 

Dustin Bickel

By Charumini de Silva

Sri Lanka’s maritime opportunity has reached a turning point, with global shipping, manufacturing and US maritime officials urging Colombo to move with urgency from being a successful transshipment hub to becoming a digitally enabled, high-speed and value-adding supply-chain hub.

From cutting Customs clearance waiting times and digitising supply chains to developing value-added logistics, green-fuel bunkering and stronger port-to-port links, speakers at the Colombo International Maritime and Logistics Conference 2026 said Sri Lanka’s next challenge was no longer identifying its maritime potential, but converting it into competitive advantage.

The discussion at the inauguration of the 8th edition of the Conference under the theme "Building a World Around Us", held alongside the 15th anniversary of the Shippers’ Academy last Wednesday featured; US FMC Commissioner Robert J. Harvey, AP Moller (Maersk) Singapore Managing Director René Piil Pedersen, Brandix Lanka CEO Ashroff Omar, and US Embassy in Colombo Indo-Pacific Coordinator Dustin Bickel. The session was moderated by Shippers' Academy Colombo CEO and CIMC Events Founder Rohan Masakorala.

Below are excerpts of the panel discussion: 

Q: Can you give us a brief on what's happening in the fashion industry? With the global maritime sector facing supply chain challenges, what are your views on Sri Lanka and its maritime ecosystem? How would you like to see it evolve over the next 25 years as your company scales to the next level?

Ashroff: I think, looking at the way things are moving, a 25-year horizon is premature, because things are changing extremely fast. If you look at just the next three to five years, everything in our industry is being reshaped by customer demand. It's no longer just about cost and delivery; now it's cost, speed, and flexibility, often with smaller order volumes. 

To meet that demand, logistics has to be treated as an integral, end-to-end part of the process, not something we hand off to a forwarder and forget about. Fashion moves so fast now that a garment has almost become perishable: if it doesn't arrive on time, it loses its value.

With the advent of AI, I believe current usage in our industry is under 0.5%. We might save five days in production, but the goods can then sit at port or with freight forwarders for another 10 days, erasing all those gains. Without a fully digital supply chain, that inefficiency will keep costing us.

As an industry, we are proposing that Customs clearance be pre-cleared straight from the manufacturing plant, so shipments aren't held up in documentation or other processes once goods are ready to move, those steps need to be digitised entirely. I'm not proposing faster ships; I'm saying we can eliminate the waiting time in the process. If we do that over the next year or two, we can gain much better leverage and competitiveness against other countries.

Q: Turning to Sri Lanka specifically, over the coming three to five years, what would you like to see change from service providers and policymakers? Where is your industry facing the biggest challenges right now?

Ashroff: As I said, speed is now critical, waiting time has to stop. That requires strong Government support to ensure digitalisation is executed quickly. Once goods are produced, they need to be shipped out as fast as possible. What we need are quick, practical steps rather than grand plans that don't get delivered. I think that's a view shared across the industry. We should be talking about the next five years, not 25 years.

Q: From your regional vantage point in Singapore, what critical physical and digital infrastructure changes should emerging hubs like Sri Lanka be focusing on? How can that East Asian experience be applied to South Asia, and specifically to Sri Lanka?

René: At Maersk, we operate across several parts of this industry. We're known primarily as a global shipping line, but we also operate terminals. As many of you know, we are a partner at South Asia Gateway Terminals (SAGT) in Colombo and we are active in landside logistics as well, including warehousing and distribution centres.

Fundamentally, what we do is enable trade. As one of the earlier speakers, I believe the Governor of the Western Province pointed out, we create opportunities for exporters and importers. It's the reason consumers in the US can buy apparel manufactured right here in Sri Lanka.

Looking at Sri Lanka alongside other hubs in Southeast Asia, Singapore, but also Vietnam and Malaysia, the real transformation happens when you combine a hub with strong logistics capability. That combination creates an ecosystem far bigger than the sum of its parts, and it's also what attracts FDI. A country like Sri Lanka has the opportunity to capture a much larger share of the value chain, not just in distribution, but in value-added services.

Take Singapore as an example. Scotch whisky exporters ship bottles into Singapore, store them in a free trade zone, and the labelling is finalised depending on the final destination, different requirements for the Philippines versus Jakarta, for instance. That value-added service is captured by Singapore, even though it doesn't produce whisky itself. Sri Lanka sits right on a major global trade route, which is exactly the kind of opportunity that presents.

Q: Given your background in maritime law and the Federal Maritime Commission's ongoing focus on global chokepoints and supply chain resilience — how do you approach your role at the FMC, and how do you manage disruptions to navigation and international trade affecting US supply chains?

Robert: American cargo doesn't begin its journey when it reaches one of our ports, it often begins thousands of miles away, frequently in a place like Sri Lanka. If our global supply chains had the resilience of the Sri Lankan people, we'd be in much better shape.

We investigate chokepoints on an ongoing basis, I can't speak to specific cases, but chokepoints can occur anywhere: at the origin of cargo, along shipping routes, at the terminal on arrival, or after cargo leaves the terminal gates. As a regulatory agency taking an increasingly assertive stance, we investigate any chokepoints that negatively impact American cargo, and we enforce where necessary.

Beyond our regulatory role, we also have enforcement authority, and we function in a quasi-judicial capacity, we operate transparently, so the results of our regulatory cases, fines, and the decisions we render in disputes between private parties are all publicly available. We have seven full-time administrative law judges handling these cases. Chokepoints are just one of many areas we monitor, but a very important one.

Q: As a country, how would you suggest the Government of Sri Lanka work more closely with the Federal Maritime Commission?

Robert: I think we continue doing what we've started, this kind of exchange, where you visit us and we're here in turn. It's an exchange of ideas and approaches to enforcement. We're happy to share that information; it's publicly available, but we're also glad to discuss it one-on-one. We'll work with anyone in the world to ensure American cargo isn't negatively affected and anytime you want to reach out, you can call me or the Chair directly.

Q: You've been based here for a couple of years now, having previously worked in South India as well. Given your broader regional perspective — where can Sri Lanka improve in terms of technology and other areas, in ways that would also benefit US exporters?

Dustin: Over the past three years, I've had the pleasure of watching Sri Lanka's port sector grow, watching terminals come to life, including the development of both WCT and ECT. The United States has partnered with the Sri Lankan Government and the Ports Authority for some time, but our focus has centred on the Port of Colombo, looking at how we can improve efficiency and strengthen both bilateral and broader Indo-Pacific trade. Everyone here knows Colombo is South Asia's predominant transshipment hub, and until relatively recently, it was one of the only deepwater transshipment hubs in all of South Asia. The port handled over 8 million TEUs last year, and SLPA has projects underway to expand capacity to 14–15 million TEUs within just a few years. As other speakers mentioned, roughly half a million of those 8 million TEUs represent US-inbound and outbound cargo, amounting to tens of billions of dollars flowing into our economy.

So our focus is on streamlining cargo handling at the Port of Colombo, because greater efficiency translates directly into reduced shipping costs, which benefits US manufacturers shipping through Colombo, and ultimately US consumers, since those savings get passed down. This isn't purely altruistic support for Sri Lanka's ports; it's a genuine win-win for both economies.

Some of the work we've done with the Sri Lankan Government and SLPA includes facilitating regional engagements that bring port sector stakeholders from across South Asia together, to build relationships, improve communication between ports, and enable them to call on each other for support when needed. We also run workshops and training programs involving multiple countries.

On cargo security, the US Department of Energy runs a program called the Nuclear Smuggling Detection and Deterrence Program, some of you may know it as "Megaports." This strengthens the port's ability to scan containers and prevent the movement of radiological materials, helping keep the whole world safer.

We're also building port-to-port relationships. Last year, we facilitated a memorandum of cooperation between the Port of Colombo and the Virginia Port Authority, and we're looking to expand these partnerships with more American ports, enabling knowledge exchange and shared development. Through these exchanges, workshops, training, and the provision of key equipment some of which we expect to announce in the coming months, the US Government continues to demonstrate its commitment to Sri Lanka's ports and maritime sector, and to advancing the shared prosperity of both our countries.

Q:On the subject of US tariffs, everyone wants to know how you manage this, especially given Laura's access to President Trump. How do you actually navigate it?

Ashroff: That's a tough question. The advantage for Sri Lanka's apparel sector has been that, relative to our competitors, we're on par, if not ahead. That's helped us in the short term. Whether that's sustainable long term is the real question, which is exactly why fixing our infrastructure and improving our speed to compete matters so much.

We can't control what tariff regime the US, Europe, or any other country chooses to impose. We can only control how competitive we make ourselves relative to our peers. Some competing countries have full duty-free access, but face other disadvantages; otherwise, there would be no exports coming out of this part of the world at all. Our Government needs to keep that relationship strong enough that we're not disadvantaged, and I think, so far, that's been managed reasonably well. Beyond that, we need to look inward, strengthening ports and the supply chain to reduce costs and improve efficiency is something entirely within our control.

Q: As the shipping industry moves toward greening its fleet, in line with global decarbonisation goals — what do you expect from the Port of Colombo on that front?

René: Decarbonisation remains high on our agenda, though the conversation has shifted somewhat with high oil prices, in many regions it's increasingly about energy independence rather than just emissions.

Being a hub creates an opportunity to be more than just a transshipment gateway, it can also become a bunkering hub. Some countries have already capitalised on this; Singapore, again, is a strong example, supported by its refining capacity. Being able to offer future fuels including; green fuels specifically creates real stickiness, making a location more attractive to shipowners like us.

That said, the key question for Sri Lanka is whether it can produce fuel domestically, green molecules, in particular and whether it wants to allocate that capacity to the international shipping industry. Becoming a bunkering hub is a genuine opportunity, and one that could also benefit the local economy by creating jobs and building new skills.

Q: So you see a role for Sri Lanka in the green shipping transition?

René: Absolutely. As I mentioned, Sri Lanka sits right next to one of the world's major shipping highways. As a shipowner, we operate around 150 vessels flying the Singapore flag, I'd welcome the opportunity to bunker here. I've discussed this with the Minister directly, and I recognise it isn't a simple undertaking. But it is a real opportunity, and if fuel can be sourced regionally and made available here, it would be an attractive option for other shipowners too.

More broadly, we have a strong ambition to decarbonise our entire supply chain, whether that's warehouses, port operations, or logistics. In several countries, we're introducing EV trucks for container transport, and all our new terminals are being built with decarbonisation and renewable energy use in mind. This is both a genuine commitment on our part and something that strengthens our competitiveness.

Q: Your CV mentions an interest in quantum maritime solutions, fleet optimisation, secure communications, and so on. Can you explain what that involves?

Robert: I'm a securities lawyer by background, but a scientist. In a prior role, I served as President of the Florida Opportunity Fund, the State's venture capital fund, where we were an active technology investor, including in quantum computing. I believe quantum will be one of the next major developments in maritime, particularly around communications and predictive maintenance. I recently attended the White House's AI summit, which also touched on quantum.

I'm a strong believer in backing technology and innovation. As a regulator, even as we pursue aggressive enforcement, I'm always mindful of the business implications of our decisions. We don't want our regulations to hamper innovation or discourage investment, because without investment, you don't get innovation. The rules need to apply equally to every player in the maritime ecosystem, and if a quantum-focused maritime startup is looking for a base, Colombo could be a genuinely attractive option, provided the regulatory and investment framework is transparent enough for investors to feel confident. That principle applies to every level of the supply chain. I'm sure René would say the same about how his terminals are run.

Q: Finally, what's your closing message to this conference?

Dustin: We see real opportunity in Sri Lanka's port sector, and on behalf of the US Government, we look forward to continuing to work with Sri Lanka, SLPA, and the Ministry to help grow this industry — because ultimately, we all benefit.

Ashroff: I think conferences like this can help push us beyond simply being a maritime hub, toward becoming a high-speed supply chain. I hope your deliberations over the next couple of days move us further in that direction.

René: Seize the day. You're sitting on a tremendous opportunity here, your geographic position, and your standing as an important hub for the region and globally. That's exactly why we have the FMC's representation here today. Seize the day, Sri Lanka has the opportunity to make this happen.

Robert: There's a tremendous opportunity here, but it now comes down to execution. Think of the country as a business; you need a plan, and at some point you need to execute it with urgency. Change is happening quickly, so there has to be a real sense of urgency to move things forward. You're blessed with an opportunity, now it's time to execute.

title: SLANA calls for urgent fix to Colombo terminal charges as NVOCC sector loses regional competitiveness | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:46
-     - 52

Sri Lanka Association of NVOCC Agents Chairperson Swabha Wickramasinghe says empty-container backlogs, rising terminal charges threaten sector competitiveness and require urgent policy action

 Notes over 75 NVOCC lines strengthen Sri Lanka’s regional connectivity across India, China, the Far East and Middle East

 Asserts geopolitical and shipping disruptions are heightening need for flexible, alternative trade routes

 Insists on predictable policies, efficient processes to materialise Colombo’s ambition of becoming a regional logistics hub

By Charumini de Silva

SLANA Chairperson Swabha Wickramasinghe

Sri Lanka’s NVOCC sector is losing ground to competing regional markets amid continued uncertainty over terminal handling charges (THC), with the industry warning that the issue is making Colombo commercially less attractive for regional shipping services and putting pressure on predominantly SME operators.

Sri Lanka Association of NVOCC Agents (SLANA) Chairperson Swabha Wickramasinghe made the call at the association’s 9th Annual General Meeting, calling the Government to expedite a promised committee to examine the THC issue and deliver a practical solution.

Wickramasinghe, who became SLANA’s first elected female Chairperson in 2024 and was re-elected for a third consecutive term, said the association had repeatedly raised concerns over the treatment of THC as a separate land-based cost in international markets, while Sri Lanka continued with a different practice.

“One of the main reasons is the continued difficulty in collecting the Colombo terminal charges as a separate land-based cost,” she stressed.

She warned that the issue was no longer simply about the charge itself, but the broader economics of operating NVOCC services from Sri Lanka.

“When Sri Lanka becomes less commercially attractive compared with other regional destinations, the consequences eventually reach our members,” Wickramasinghe said.

More than 75 NVOCC lines currently operate in Sri Lanka, supporting regional connectivity across India, China, the Far East, Middle East and beyond. Wickramasinghe said their role had become particularly important given the regional nature of Sri Lanka’s trade, with China and India accounting for around 44% of imports, while India is the country’s second-largest export market.

She said NVOCC operators had also demonstrated their importance during the COVID-19 pandemic, when major carriers prioritised long-haul routes and NVOCCs helped sustain regional trade flows.

But the sector is now facing a combination of geopolitical conflicts, sanctions, changing trade policies and shipping-route disruptions, making flexibility and alternative connectivity increasingly important.

“Whatever happens in the world, trade must continue to move and we must be prepared to keep it moving,” she said.

Wickramasinghe asserted that the majority of SLANA members were SMEs employing people, paying taxes and investing in their operations, making the competitiveness issue broader than the profitability of a single industry.

“This is not simply a request to improve the profitability of one sector. It is about creating a fair and internationally competitive operating environment for Sri Lankan businesses,” she said.

Wickramasinghe also called for an urgent resolution to the continuing issue of uncleared empty containers at the Port of Colombo, noting delays were preventing containers from being released to their designated carriers. SLANA has been engaging with Sri Lanka Customs and the Ports Ministry and is seeking a practical solution, including through a possible Cabinet paper.

The association is also monitoring proposed rates and charges for services provided by terminal operators, urging that inland and terminal-related charges remain reasonable and competitive with regional ports.

Despite the challenges, Wickramasinghe said Colombo’s expanding capacity offered a major opportunity to move beyond transhipment and develop into a regional logistics hub integrating port capacity, connectivity, warehousing, distribution and other value-added services.

“The bigger opportunity goes beyond simply handling more containers,” she said.

For that opportunity to materialise, however, she stressed that businesses need confidence, predictable policies and transparent processes.

“As SLANA, we will continue to work constructively with the Government and all stakeholders to build a stronger, more competitive and efficient maritime and logistics industry in Sri Lanka,” Wickramasinghe said.

- Pix by Upul Abayasekara
